---
title: "Categorical biomarkers"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  out.width = "100%",
  dpi = 96
)
```

Not every repeated measurement is a number. A symptom can be graded (none,
mild, severe), a finding can be present or absent, a disease can be staged.
BJM accepts such **ordinal** biomarkers, including **binary** ones, next to
continuous ones, and uses them for every prediction: the risk of an event,
the future category of the biomarker itself, and simulated futures.

| Step | Function | With a categorical biomarker |
|---|---|---|
| Fit | `longitudinalSub()` | an ordered-factor response is fit as an ordinal biomarker |
| Predict | `predictRisk()` | the observed categories inform the risk |
| Predict | `predictLongitudinal()` | the probability of each category at a future time |
| Plot | `predictPlot()`, `riskPlot()` | the categories on the biomarker axis |
| Simulate | `simulateTrajectory()` | simulated categories |

Fitting an ordinal biomarker needs the **ordinal** package (in `Suggests`):

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(BJM)
data(pbc3)
requireNamespace("ordinal", quietly = TRUE)
```

## How BJM models a category

Behind each ordinal measurement, BJM assumes a continuous *latent score*
that follows a linear mixed model, just like a continuous biomarker, and that
is cut into the observed categories at estimated thresholds. This is a probit
cumulative link mixed model, fit with `ordinal::clmm()`. A binary biomarker is
the special case of two categories and one threshold.

The latent scores and the continuous biomarkers share one joint
random-effects distribution (a Gaussian copula). So a patient's categories
tell the model about their continuous biomarkers and the other way round, and
both inform the event risk. `longitudinalSub()` estimates this joint
covariance by maximum likelihood, with an EM algorithm that integrates over
the ordinal random effects by adaptive Gauss--Hermite quadrature; with more
than four ordinal random effects in all it switches to a stochastic
approximation EM.

## The data

`edema` in `pbc3` is recorded at every visit in three ordered categories: no
edema, edema without diuretics or resolved by them, and edema despite
diuretics. We give the categories short names and make the column an
**ordered factor**, which is how BJM recognizes an ordinal biomarker. The
order of the levels is the order of the categories.

```{r data}
pbc3$edema <- factor(pbc3$edema, labels = c("none", "controlled", "persistent"),
                     ordered = TRUE)
table(pbc3$edema)
```

Edema changes during follow-up for many patients:

```{r data-changes}
changes <- tapply(as.integer(pbc3$edema), pbc3$id, function(x) length(unique(x)) > 1)
sum(changes)
```

## Fitting

The survival sub-model is the usual one, here with competing risks (death
and transplantation, see the [Competing risks](competing-risks.html)
article):

```{r survival-sub}
survival_fit <- survivalSub(pbc3[!duplicated(pbc3$id), ],
                            Surv(years, status3) ~ age + sex,
                            status4 ~ years + age + sex)
```

The ordinal biomarker gets a formula and random effects like any other.
Because `edema` is an ordered factor, `longitudinalSub()` fits it as ordinal
and `serBilir` as continuous; `biomarker_type = c("continuous", "ordinal")`
would say the same explicitly. The model has no intercept: the thresholds
take its place.

```{r longitudinal-sub, warning = FALSE}
long_fit <- longitudinalSub(
  pbc3[pbc3$status3 == 1, ],
  list(serBilir = serBilir ~ year + age + sex + years + years:year,
       edema    = edema ~ year + age + years + years:year),
  list(serBilir = ~ year | id, edema = ~ 1 | id)
)
long_fit$biomarker_type
```

(`ordinal::clmm()` may warn about a non-finite log-likelihood at an
intermediate iteration of its optimizer; this one does, and the warning is
hidden above. It is harmless when the fit converges, as it does here: the
largest gradient at the optimum is below 0.01.)

```{r print-fit}
long_fit
```

For `edema`, the printed fit shows the coefficients of the latent score and
the two thresholds between the three categories. Edema becomes more likely
over follow-up (`year`) and the closer a patient is to the event (`years`).
The last table is the joint covariance of the random effects: the edema
intercept is positively correlated with the bilirubin intercept, so patients
with more edema tend to have higher bilirubin.

### A binary biomarker

A two-level factor is a binary biomarker, fit the same way. Here `ascites`
(`No`/`Yes`) is added as a third biomarker:

```{r binary, warning = FALSE}
long_fit_3 <- longitudinalSub(
  pbc3[pbc3$status3 == 1, ],
  list(serBilir ~ year + age + sex + years + years:year,
       edema ~ year + age + years + years:year,
       ascites ~ year + years),
  list(~ year | id, ~ 1 | id, ~ 1 | id)
)
long_fit_3$biomarker_type
round(cov2cor(long_fit_3$Sigma_fit), 2)
```

Edema and ascites are strongly correlated (0.85): both reflect fluid
retention.

## Predicting the event risk with `predictRisk()`

Patient 2 had no edema at the first four visits, and controlled edema at the
visit just before year 5:

```{r patient}
patient <- pbc3[pbc3$id == 2 & pbc3$year <= 5, ]
patient$years <- NA
patient$status4 <- NA
patient[, c("year", "serBilir", "edema")]
```

`predictRisk()` is called as usual. With an ordinal biomarker, each
patient's likelihood includes the probability of their observed categories.
With one ordinal random effect, as here, BJM computes it by numerical
integration over that random effect, so the results are exact and the same
on every run.

```{r predict-risk}
risk <- predictRisk(list(patient, patient), long_fit, survival_fit,
                    prediction_time = 5, horizon = 3, time_variable = "year",
                    survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list())
risk
```

The categories matter. Had the last visit shown no edema, the predicted risk
of death within three years would be about half as large:

```{r what-if}
no_edema <- patient
no_edema$edema[nrow(no_edema)] <- "none"
risk_no_edema <- predictRisk(list(no_edema, no_edema), long_fit, survival_fit,
                             prediction_time = 5, horizon = 3, time_variable = "year",
                             survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list())
c(observed = unname(risk$risk_prob_1), if_no_edema = unname(risk_no_edema$risk_prob_1))
```

The categories in the prediction data are matched to those of the fit by
their labels, so a character column or a factor with its levels in a
different order works too; a category the model was not fit with is an
error.

## Predicting the future category with `predictLongitudinal()`

For an ordinal biomarker, `predictLongitudinal()` predicts the probability
of each category at `prediction_time + horizon`, for a patient still
event-free then. Here for three patients, one year after year 3:

```{r predict-longitudinal}
three <- pbc3[pbc3$id %in% c(2, 4, 5) & pbc3$year <= 3, ]
three$years <- NA
three$status4 <- NA
edema_pred <- predictLongitudinal(bio_i = 2, list(three, three), long_fit, survival_fit,
                                  prediction_time = 3, horizon = 1, time_variable = "year",
                                  survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list())
edema_pred
```

In the returned object, `Y_density` holds the probabilities (one column per
patient), `Y_all` the category codes `1, 2, 3` with their labels in the
`"category_labels"` attribute, and `Y_predict` the code of the most likely
category. `plot()` draws the probabilities:

```{r plot-longitudinal, fig.alt = "Bar charts of the predicted probabilities of no, controlled and persistent edema one year after year 3, one panel per patient: patient 2 most likely has none (about 0.79), patient 4 persistent (about 0.78), and patient 5 is split between controlled (0.41) and persistent (0.50)."}
plot(edema_pred)
```

With `bio_i = NULL` every biomarker is predicted in one call, continuous and
ordinal alike:

```{r predict-both}
both <- predictLongitudinal(bio_i = NULL, list(three, three), long_fit, survival_fit,
                            prediction_time = 3, horizon = 1, time_variable = "year",
                            survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list())
names(both)
both$edema$Y_density
```

## Plotting a patient's predictions

`predictPlot()` shows the history of one biomarker, chosen with `bio_his`,
with its categories on the vertical axis, the risks of the two event types,
and the predicted category probabilities as the horizon grows, as circles
whose size is the probability:

```{r predict-plot, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5.5, fig.alt = "Prediction plot for patient 2 at year 5 with edema on the vertical axis: no edema at the first four visits and controlled edema just before year 5; after year 5, circles show the predicted probabilities of each category up to year 8, with controlled and none most likely and persistent growing; the risk of death rises to about 0.43 by year 8 and that of transplantation stays near 0."}
predictPlot(list(patient, patient), long_fit, survival_fit,
            prediction_time = 5, horizon = seq(0, 3, 0.5), time_variable = "year",
            survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list(),
            bio_his = 2, bio_pred = 2)
```

`riskPlot()` moves the landmark instead; the risk of death rises when the
edema appears:

```{r risk-plot, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5.5, fig.alt = "Patient 2's edema history, none until year 2 and controlled just before year 5, with the predicted one-year risks of death and transplantation at landmarks 1 to 5; the risk of death stays below 0.05 until year 4 and rises to about 0.1 at year 5, and transplantation stays near 0."}
riskPlot(list(patient, patient), long_fit, survival_fit,
         prediction_time = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), bio_i = 2, horizon = 1, time_variable = "year",
         survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list())
```

## Simulated futures with `simulateTrajectory()`

Simulated futures draw a latent score for the ordinal biomarker and cut it
at the thresholds, so the draws are categories:

```{r simulate}
sims <- simulateTrajectory(list(patient, patient), long_fit, survival_fit,
                           prediction_time = 5, times = seq(5, 10, 0.5), time_variable = "year",
                           survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list(),
                           n_sim = 300, seed = 1)
head(as.data.frame(sims)[, c("sim", "year", "serBilir", "edema")])
```

`plot()` shows, at each time, the share of the draws still event-free in
each category:

```{r simulate-plot, fig.alt = "Simulated futures of patient 2 from year 5 to 10 in two panels: for bilirubin, the observed values as points with simulated trajectories and a median rising from about 1 to 2; for edema, stacked bars of the share of draws in each category, with no edema falling from about half to about a quarter and persistent edema rising from about 0.1 to about 0.45."}
plot(sims)
```

## Things to watch for

* **Make the response an ordered factor**, with its levels in the order of
  the categories, or pass `biomarker_type`. A numeric column is fit as a
  continuous biomarker.
* **Formulas.** An ordinal biomarker's design matrix is built from the data
  at hand, not from the training data, so terms whose values depend on the
  other rows -- orthogonal `poly()`, `splines::ns()`/`bs()`, `factor()` --
  give wrong predictions; `longitudinalSub()` warns about them. Use
  `poly(..., raw = TRUE)`, `I(x^2)` or `log()` instead (see the
  [Nonlinear terms](nonlinear-terms.html) article).
* **Two or more ordinal random effects.** The probability of a patient's
  observed categories is then computed by Monte Carlo
  (`mvtnorm::pmvnorm()`) instead of numerical integration, with an error in
  about the fourth significant digit (each patient's draws use a fixed seed,
  so the results are still the same on every run), and predictions are
  several times slower. `n_cores` in `predictRisk()` and
  `predictLongitudinal()` spreads the patients over several cores (on Linux
  and macOS).
* **Speed.** That probability is needed at every point of the integration
  grid, so a prediction with an ordinal biomarker takes longer than with
  continuous ones only. Predicting a continuous biomarker's future value in
  a model with an ordinal one is the slowest case; fixed
  `bandcount2`/`bandcount3` values (checked with
  `checkBandcountConvergence()`) are faster than the automatic ones.
* **Random effects.** Up to four ordinal random effects in all (e.g. two
  ordinal biomarkers with a random intercept and slope each) are integrated
  by quadrature; beyond that, the stochastic approximation EM is less
  precise (random-effects variances off by about 5% in simulations).
